idiom_name: discriminator-keyed map of pure (raw) => canonical functions
implementation_notes: Nothing in the language or the standard library requires a Translator class: JSON.parse produces the raw value and a plain object (or Map) keyed by the wire discriminator holds one pure function per source format, so the router is a property lookup and the translators are ordinary functions that return the canonical object. Destructuring, default parameters and explicit field mapping do the canonicalization, and runtime validation belongs in the same step because the types are erased (typeof/Array.isArray guards, or a schema validator such as Ajv or zod). Classes and registries are still justified when a translator needs lifecycle or injected collaborators (a client, a lookup service, per-partner configuration), which is rare for pure format conversion.
pitfalls: JSON.parse accepts duplicate keys (last one wins) and returns numbers that lose precision beyond 2^53, so canonical ids and money should be strings validated as such.
Object spreads and deep merges of untrusted payloads complete a prototype-pollution attack (__proto__, constructor); map fields explicitly instead of {...defaults, ...payload} for wire data.
A plain-object registry inherits Object.prototype keys, so a payload with type: "constructor" can select a translator - use Object.hasOwn, Object.create(null) or a Map.
JSON.parse returns any, and the canonical object is only as trustworthy as the raw bytes unless a schema validator runs at the same seam.
